sentences.text: Fragmentary remains suggest that adult Liliensternus could have reached lengths of 7 to 9 meters, while other estimates place the animal at approximately 5.15 meters long and weighing about 127 kilograms.
Still other researchers suggest a maximum length of 5.20 meters and a maximum weight of 200 kilograms.

Estimates for adult Liliensternus vary, with fragmentary remains suggesting lengths of 7 to 9 meters, other estimates placing it at approximately 5.15 meters long and weighing about 127 kilograms, and still other researchers suggesting a maximum length of 5.20 meters and a maximum weight of 200 kilograms.
Measurements of the skeleton show a tibia that is 409 mm long and a femur that is 440 mm long.
The dinosaur possessed an unusually short ilium, a feature similar to the condition seen in Dilophosaurus.

Liliensternus is the best-represented Triassic theropod from Europe; however, due to conflicting size estimates ranging from approximately 5.15 meters to 9 meters, its status as one of the largest known theropods remains uncertain.
It had five fingers with smaller fourth and fifth digits, representing a possible transitional stage between five-fingered Triassic theropods and three-fingered Jurassic theropods.
Many reconstructions depict Liliensternus with a crest similar to that of Dilophosaurus, though the skull is not well known.
The type specimens were discovered near Großer Gleichberg in Thuringia, Germany.
Count Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern found these remains in the winter of 1932/1933.
Friedrich von Huene formally described Liliensternus in 1934.
The syntypes were found in marl deposits from the Late Triassic Norian stage, approximately 228 to 208 million years ago.
The name honors Count Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern, an amateur paleontologist and medical doctor.
In 1993, Gilles Cuny and Peter Galton described a new species assigned to this genus, Liliensternus airelensis.
In 2007, Martin Ezcurra and Cuny reassigned the material of L. airelensis to their own genus, Lophostropheus.
Liliensternus was an active bipedal carnivore that likely preyed on large herbivores like Plateosaurus.
Liliensternus is classified as a basal member of the Neotheropoda.
Rowe discovered in 1989 that Liliensternus is more derived than Dilophosaurus.
Originally assigned to Halticosauridae, Liliensternus is now considered a basal member of Neotheropoda.
Liliensternus lived during the Norian to Rhaetian stages, from 227.3 to 201.4 million years ago.
The only material from later strata assigned to this genus was discovered in 1913 in blue claystone of the Late Triassic Rhaetian stage in the Trossingen Formation of Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.
It is debated whether Liliensternus airelensis should remain in Liliensternus or be assigned to the separate genus Lophostropheus.
